options: `plain` then `plain`, because `s` itself is not const
`const` then `plain`
`const` then `const`
Ill-formed: the call through `const S&` is ambiguous
questions.explanation: The object expression in `call` is an lvalue of type `const S`, which can only bind to the implicit object parameter `const S&`, so the const overload runs. In `main`, `s` is a non-const lvalue, and `S&` is a better match than `const S&`, so the plain overload runs. What matters is the type of the expression left of the dot, not the type the object was originally declared with.

options: Ill-formed: an rvalue cannot bind to the non-const implicit object parameter
Well-formed
Well-formed, but modifying a temporary is undefined behavior
Ill-formed: `reset` would need an `&&` ref-qualifier
questions.explanation: For a member function declared without a ref-qualifier, [over.match.funcs] makes an exception: an rvalue may bind to the implicit object parameter even though its type is a non-const lvalue reference. That is the rule the first option forgets. Modifying a temporary during its lifetime is perfectly defined; the temporary is simply destroyed at the end of the full-expression.

questions.prompt: In C++23, this is the whole program, in one translation unit. Is it well-formed?
options: Ill-formed, no diagnostic required: `max` needs a definition outside the class
Well-formed only if the compiler constant-folds `r`
Ill-formed: a reference cannot bind to a constexpr variable
Well-formed: the in-class declaration is a definition
questions.explanation: Since C++17 a `static constexpr` data member is implicitly an inline variable, so its in-class declaration is a definition and an odr-use such as binding a reference is fine. Before C++17 the first option was correct: binding the reference odr-used `max`, and without an out-of-class definition the program typically failed to link. A plain `static const int` member is still not inline today.

options: `lvalue`
`rvalue`, because `take` only runs on rvalues
Ill-formed: the call to `sink` is ambiguous
Unspecified: it depends on whether the temporary is materialized
questions.explanation: The `&&` qualifier only decides which objects `take` may be called on. Inside the body, `name` is an id-expression naming a data member, which is an lvalue, exactly as in any other member function. To get `rvalue` you must write `sink(std::move(name))` or `sink(std::move(*this).name)`.

questions.prompt: Which marked line makes this class definition ill-formed?
options: A, because `g` is not declared yet
B, because `g` is not declared yet
C, because `size_type` is not declared yet
None of them; members are visible throughout the class
questions.explanation: Function bodies, default arguments, `noexcept` specifiers and default member initializers are complete-class contexts, where the whole class is visible, so A and B find the later `g`. A member function's return type is not such a context, so `size_type` is looked up from that point backwards and is not found, so line C is ill-formed. Line A is the tempting answer, but the `noexcept` specifier was made a complete-class context precisely so it can refer to later members.

questions.prompt: What does this C++23 program print?
options: Ill-formed: an explicit object parameter cannot be a forwarding reference
questions.explanation: `Self` is deduced at compile time from the object expression. `d` has type `Derived`, so `Self` is `Derived&`; `b` has static type `Base`, so `Self` is `Base&`, even though it refers to a `Derived`. Deducing `this` is not a virtual dispatch mechanism, which is why `2 2` is wrong. `this Self&&` is the canonical forwarding form of an explicit object parameter.

questions.prompt: In C++20, what does the lambda capture, given that `n` is a non-static data member?
options: A copy of `n`
A copy of `*this`
The `this` pointer, and this implicit capture is deprecated
Nothing: the program is ill-formed because `this` is not listed
questions.explanation: Naming `n` in the lambda means `(*this).n`, so what is implicitly captured is the entity `this`, and it is captured as a pointer even under a copy default. The closure therefore refers to the original object, which is why the first two options are tempting but wrong. C++20 deprecated implicitly capturing `this` through `[=]`; write `[=, this]` or `[*this]` to say which you mean.

questions.prompt: In C++23, what is the type of `&E::get`?
options: `int (E::*)() const`
`int (*)(const E&)`
`int (E::*)(const E&)`
Ill-formed: the address of an explicit object member function cannot be taken
questions.explanation: For an explicit object member function, the object parameter is an ordinary parameter, and [expr.unary.op] says that taking its address yields a pointer to function, not a pointer to member. So the type is `int (*)(const E&)` and you call it as `(&E::get)(e)`. The pointer-to-member type in the first option is what you get for the classic spelling `int get() const`.
